q: What do we call a person trained to travel into space?
fact: The word astronaut comes from Greek words meaning 'star sailor'.

q: What type of object is the Sun?
fact: The Sun is so big that more than a million Earths could fit inside it.

q: Which planet is third from the Sun?
fact: Earth is the only planet known to have liquid water on its surface.

q: What is it called when the Moon blocks our view of the Sun during the day?
fact: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times farther away, so they look the same size.

q: What does ISS stand for in space travel?
fact: The International Space Station zooms all the way around Earth roughly every 90 minutes.

q: NASA is the space agency of which country?
fact: NASA was set up in 1958, more than a decade before the first Moon landing.

q: What is a 'shooting star' really?
fact: Most shooting stars are made by specks of space dust no bigger than a grain of sand.

q: Which force keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
fact: Isaac Newton's ideas about gravity are said to have been inspired by a falling apple.

q: What do we call a group of stars that forms a pattern or picture in the sky?
fact: Astronomers officially recognise 88 constellations covering the whole sky.

q: Roughly how long does it take Earth to travel once around the Sun?
fact: A year is about 365 and a quarter days, which is why we add an extra day every leap year.

q: Roughly how long does it take Earth to spin once on its axis?
fact: Earth's spin is very gradually slowing down, so days were shorter when dinosaurs lived.

q: What is the name for a scientist who studies stars and planets?
fact: The Royal Observatory in Greenwich was founded for astronomers in 1675.

q: What is an icy space object that grows a glowing tail as it nears the Sun?
fact: A comet's tail always points away from the Sun, pushed back by sunlight and the solar wind.

q: What are the rocky objects that mostly orbit the Sun between Mars and Jupiter?
fact: Some asteroids even have their own tiny moons orbiting them.

q: Which planet is named after the king of the Roman gods?
fact: Jupiter is so big that all the other planets in the Solar System could fit inside it.

q: In 1969, the Apollo 11 mission landed astronauts where?
fact: The Apollo 11 crew brought back about 21 kilograms of Moon rock and dust.

q: What do astronomers use to make distant stars and planets look bigger?
fact: Galileo was one of the first people to point a telescope at the night sky, in 1609.

q: What is the name for the path one object takes around another in space?
fact: Planets' orbits are not perfect circles but slightly squashed ovals called ellipses.

q: What do we call the Moon when its whole face is lit up?
fact: There is a full moon roughly once every 29 and a half days.

q: What is the name for an astronaut from Russia?
fact: Chinese astronauts are sometimes called taikonauts, from the Chinese word for space.

q: What is Earth's only natural satellite?
fact: The Moon is very slowly drifting away from Earth, by about 3.8 centimetres a year.

q: What are the bowl-shaped dents on the Moon's surface called?
fact: Most of the Moon's craters were made by asteroids and comets crashing into it.

q: What causes day and night on Earth?
options: Earth moving away from the Sun
fact: At the equator, Earth's surface spins at more than 1,600 kilometres per hour.

q: The Moon's gravity is the main cause of what on Earth?
fact: Most coasts have two high tides and two low tides roughly every day.

q: What special outfit do astronauts wear to survive outside their spacecraft?
fact: A spacesuit is like a mini spacecraft, supplying oxygen and keeping the wearer at a safe temperature.

q: What is the name for the thin, curved shape the Moon sometimes appears as?
fact: Sunlight bounced off Earth, called earthshine, can make the dark part of a crescent moon faintly glow.

q: What name is given to the Sun and all the planets that travel around it?
fact: 'Solar' comes from 'sol', the Latin word for the Sun.

q: What does UFO stand for?
fact: Before the term UFO caught on, mystery objects in the sky were often called 'flying saucers'.

q: Moonlight is really light reflected from what?
fact: The Moon's surface is actually quite dark, reflecting only about 12% of the sunlight that hits it.

q: What is the layer of gases surrounding Earth called?
fact: The air we breathe is mostly nitrogen, with oxygen making up about a fifth.

q: Apollo astronauts planted which country's flag on the Moon?
fact: With no wind or rain on the Moon, the astronauts' footprints could last for millions of years.

q: What is the name for a huge group of billions of stars, like the Milky Way?
fact: The Andromeda Galaxy is so far away that its light takes over two million years to reach us.

q: What is the Moon mainly made of?
fact: Many scientists think the Moon formed from debris after a Mars-sized object hit the young Earth.

q: Which of these is classed as a dwarf planet?
fact: Pluto is smaller than Earth's Moon.

q: What vehicle is used to launch astronauts into space?
fact: A rocket blasts hot gas out of its back end, which pushes the rocket the opposite way.
